summary: Defines version 3 of the Entity MIB, which lets one SNMP agent describe the multiple physical and logical entities it manages, such as chassis, modules and ports. It obsoletes version 2 from RFC 2737. This standards-track document was itself replaced by RFC 6933.

eli5.summary: A big network box is made of many pieces, like cards and fans. This memo gives a standard way for the box to list all its parts so a manager can see what is inside.

subtitle: A standard SNMP table that lists the physical parts of a device and the logical entities that use them.

tldr.problem: One SNMP agent can manage several logical entities, such as multiple bridges, repeaters or OSPF instances, inside one physical device, and a manager needs a standard way to tell what is there.
tldr.mechanism: The Entity MIB defines tables for physical entities, logical entities and the mappings between them, plus a last-change timestamp and a change notification. Version 3 adds a cpu class, a manufacturing date, extra URIs and a PhysicalIndexOrZero convention.
tldr.outcome: Managers get one standard inventory and containment model for a device. This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 6933.

today: RFC 4133 was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 2737 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 6933, so the current Entity MIB specification is there.

sections.title: Why an Entity MIB
sections.content:
Some devices run several copies of the same MIB under a single SNMP agent: multiple bridges, multiple repeaters, or several OSPF backbone areas that share the same area-id. The RFC describes this as one "overall" physical entity that houses several logical entities. A manager needs to know exactly which logical entities the agent manages so it can address the right one.

The first Entity MIB was RFC 2037. Version 2 (RFC 2737) added non-volatile, administratively assigned identifiers for physical components and aligned the MIB with the SNMPv3 administrative framework. Version 3 adds a way to identify CPUs, a textual convention for an index value or zero, a manufacturing date and additional URIs. The MIB is written in SMIv2.
sections.eli5: One machine can pretend to be several smaller machines. The manager needs a list that says which pretend machines exist and which real parts they use.

sections.title: Key Terms: Entities, Scopes and Containment
sections.content:
A physical entity is an identifiable physical resource such as a port, backplane, sensor, daughter-card, power supply or the overall chassis. A logical entity is a managed function set such as a router, bridge or print server, represented by at most one instance of a particular set of MIB objects. Zero or more logical entities may use a physical resource.

A naming scope is the set of information reachable through one SNMP operation. For SNMPv1 it is identified by entLogicalCommunity; for SNMPv3 the term is a context. The containment tree is built by following entPhysicalContainedIn up to a value of zero, which means no further containment. The MIB does not cover proxy relationships, and it is explicitly not a replacement for a Chassis MIB.
sections.eli5: Think of a toy box (the device) with smaller boxes inside it. Each box has a number, and you can follow the boxes from the smallest up to the biggest.

sections.title: The Physical Entity Table
sections.content:
The entPhysicalTable has one row per physical entity and MUST always have a row for an overall entity, which should have class stack(11), chassis(3) or module(9). Each row is indexed by an arbitrary small integer and holds a description, a type, and optionally the index of the entity that contains it.

Later versions added more attributes: hardware, firmware and software revisions, serial number, manufacturer name, model name and a field-replaceable flag; plus three writable strings, entPhysicalAlias (a non-volatile identifier), entPhysicalAssetID and entPhysicalSerialNum. Version 3 adds entPhysicalMfgDate and entPhysicalUris, which can hold one or more URIs such as the CLEI URN example URN:CLEI:D4CE18B7AA, separated by white space.

The PhysicalClass convention gives the kind of hardware: other, unknown, chassis, backplane, container, powerSupply, fan, sensor, module, port, stack and, new in version 3, cpu. Removable things such as modules, fans and power supplies should be modeled inside a container, including empty slots.
sections.eli5: Every part gets a row in a big list, like a parts list with a name, a model, a serial number and a note saying which bigger part it sits inside.

sections.title: Logical Entities and Mapping Tables
sections.content:
The entLogicalTable has one row per logical entity, with a name, description and type, plus what is needed to reach its management information: a community name for community-based SNMP, or an SnmpEngineID and context name pair for SNMPv3. If an agent represents multiple logical entities it must implement this group; for a single logical entity or a single naming scope it may be omitted.

Three mapping tables tie things together. entLPMappingTable maps logical entities to the physical components that support them; one logical entity can use several components and several can share one. entAliasMappingTable maps logical and physical index pairs to object identifiers from other MIBs, so a port in the Interfaces MIB (ifIndex) or a repeater port can be located in the physical hierarchy. entPhysicalContainsTable lets a manager quickly find all children of a given physical entity.
sections.eli5: One list names the pretend machines. Other lists say which real parts each one uses, and where each network port sits in the box.

sections.title: Change Tracking and Multiple Agents
sections.content:
The general group holds one scalar, entLastChangeTime, the sysUptime value when any part of the Entity MIB configuration last changed. The entConfigChange notification is sent when it changes and can trigger a manager to re-poll the tables. An agent should not send more than one such notification-event in a throttling interval; five seconds is the suggested default. A manager should still check entLastChangeTime periodically to catch missed notifications.

If several agents exist in one device, each may implement the Entity MIB independently; their instances need not be equivalent or even consistent. Most objects are read-only, a deliberate choice to limit scope.

The RFC gives two worked examples with full object values. The first is a router chassis with two slots, each holding a 3-port router/bridge module, with two logical OSPF instances and two logical bridges. The second is a repeater setup. In the first example the chassis row has entPhysicalContainedIn of 0 and class chassis(3), each slot is a container(5) contained in the chassis, and so on down to the ports.

These examples show how the containment tree, logical table and mapping tables fit together for real hardware.
sections.eli5: When something in the box changes, it rings a bell, but not too often. The manager also checks the clock now and then in case it missed the bell.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects are read-write or read-create, so unprotected SET operations can harm network operation. Even reading is sensitive: the physical description, vendor type, revisions, serial number, manufacturer and model reveal what each component is, the asset ID may expose configured identifiers, and logical entity objects expose community names, network addresses and SNMP context information.

The RFC says it is important to control GET access to these objects and possibly encrypt them. SNMPv1 alone is not secure, even on a secure network. Implementers are advised to use the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) and View-based Access Control Model (RFC 3415).
sections.eli5: The parts list tells strangers exactly what is inside your box, so only trusted people should be allowed to read it or change it.
